```{python}
#| label: setup
import sys, warnings
sys.path.insert(0, "../slides")
warnings.filterwarnings("ignore")

from plotstyle import setup, CL
plt = setup()

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import statsmodels.api as sm
import statsmodels.formula.api as smf
from sklearn.metrics import (roc_curve, precision_recall_curve, roc_auc_score,
                             average_precision_score)
from sklearn.calibration import calibration_curve

loans = pd.read_parquet("../data/loans.parquet")
wine  = pd.read_parquet("../data/redwines.parquet")

m = smf.logit("default ~ fico + int_rate + np.log(revol_bal + 1)", data=loans).fit(disp=0)
p = m.predict(loans).to_numpy()
y = loans["default"].to_numpy()
BASE = y.mean()
```

## Learning objectives

By the end you should be able to:

::: {.tight}
- Say **why** a linear model cannot support a binary decision, and show it on a plot
- Fit a logistic regression in Python and report an **odds ratio** and an **average marginal effect**
- Explain why **accuracy** is the wrong metric under imbalance, and what to use instead
- Derive the cost-optimal **threshold**, and defend the cost ratio behind it
- Recognise **miscalibration**, and why it breaks a cost calculation
:::

# 1 · What this adds {background-color="#16181A" style="color:#F7F6F3"}

## Where we have got to

| Session | What you could do afterwards |
|---|---|
| **02** | Fit a line, and know what "controlling for" means geometrically |
| **03** | Attach an honest standard error to it |
| **04** | Say whether it will hold on data you have not seen |
| **05** | Handle more predictors than you can defend individually |

::: {.muted}
All four assume the thing you are predicting is a **number**.
:::

## What changes today

The outcome is a **yes or no**, and somebody has to **act** on it.

::: {.check}
That second half is new. Sessions 02–05 end with an estimate. This session ends with a
**decision** — fund the loan or refuse it — and a decision needs something none of the earlier
methods supplied: a **threshold**, which comes from economics, not from the data.
:::

## The one-sentence version

> Sessions 02–05 taught you to produce a number.
> **Session 06 is the first time the number has to become an action.**

::: {.muted}
Everything awkward in this session follows from that step — and almost every applied mistake comes
from taking it without noticing.
:::

# 2 · An example {background-color="#16181A" style="color:#F7F6F3"}

## Lending Club

A peer-to-peer marketplace: individuals lend to individuals, and the platform prices the risk.

::: {.tight}
- **9,578** three-year loans funded through LendingClub.com
- **May 2007 – February 2010**
- Outcome: the loan was **not fully repaid** — default, or charged off
:::

> **The question a lender actually has:** *which of these applications should I fund?*

# 3 · Why a straight line fails {background-color="#16181A" style="color:#F7F6F3"}

## Try it anyway

Regress the 0/1 outcome on FICO by ordinary least squares — the Session 02 estimator, unchanged.

```python
import statsmodels.api as sm
X   = sm.add_constant(loans[["fico"]])
lpm = sm.OLS(loans["default"], X).fit()
```

::: {.muted}
This is the **linear probability model**. Economists use it, and for an average effect it is
defensible.
:::

## Look at what it predicts

```{python}
lpm = sm.OLS(y, sm.add_constant(loans[["fico"]])).fit()
mlog = smf.logit("default ~ fico", data=loans).fit(disp=0)

grid = np.linspace(loans.fico.min() - 40, loans.fico.max() + 40, 300)
lin  = lpm.params.iloc[0] + lpm.params.iloc[1] * grid
lg   = 1 / (1 + np.exp(-(mlog.params.iloc[0] + mlog.params.iloc[1] * grid)))

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.axhspan(-0.18, 0, color=CL.warn, alpha=.10)
ax.axhspan(1, 1.18, color=CL.warn, alpha=.10)
ax.axhline(0, color=CL.muted, lw=.9); ax.axhline(1, color=CL.muted, lw=.9)
ax.plot(grid, lin, color=CL.warn, lw=2.4)
ax.plot(grid, lg,  color=CL.accent, lw=2.4)
ax.text(grid[8], lin[8] + .07, "linear probability model", color=CL.warn, fontweight="600")
ax.text(grid[150], lg[150] + .12, "logistic", color=CL.accent, fontweight="600")
ax.text(grid[-105], -.13, "impossible: P < 0", color=CL.warn, fontsize=8.5)
ax.set_ylim(-.18, 1.18); ax.set_xlabel("FICO score"); ax.set_ylabel("P(default)")
plt.show()
```

::: {.warn}
The straight line crosses zero: for high-FICO applicants it predicts a **negative probability of
default** — here as low as **−0.08**.
:::

## Why that is fatal for a decision

::: {.tight}
- A probability below 0 or above 1 **cannot be acted on** — you cannot multiply it by a cost
- The errors are heteroskedastic **by construction**: the variance is $p(1-p)$
- The fit is dragged by points far from the boundary, where nothing is being decided
:::

::: {.check}
For an *average effect* the LPM survives. For an *individual decision* it does not — and this
session is about decisions.
:::

# 4 · The logistic curve {background-color="#16181A" style="color:#F7F6F3"}

## Bend the line into the unit interval

$$\log\frac{p(x)}{1-p(x)} = x^\top\beta
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
p(x) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-x^\top\beta}}$$

::: {.check}
The **log-odds** on the left is free to run from $-\infty$ to $+\infty$, so a linear model is safe
there. The probability on the right is then squeezed into $(0,1)$ automatically.
:::

## What the squeeze looks like

```{python}
z = np.linspace(-6, 6, 400)
sig = 1 / (1 + np.exp(-z))
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.plot(z, sig, color=CL.accent, lw=2.6)
ax.axhline(0, color=CL.line); ax.axhline(1, color=CL.line)
ax.axhline(.5, color=CL.muted, ls=":", lw=1)
ax.axvline(0, color=CL.muted, ls=":", lw=1)
ax.plot([0], [.5], "o", color=CL.ink, ms=7)
ax.text(-5.9, .72, "steepest here — a unit of $x^{\\top}\\beta$\nmoves $p$ a great deal",
        color=CL.ink, fontsize=8.5)
ax.annotate("flat — the same unit\nbarely moves $p$", xy=(4.4, .988), xytext=(1.5, .55),
            color=CL.muted, fontsize=8.5,
            arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="->", color=CL.muted, lw=.9))
ax.set_xlabel("$x^{\\top}\\beta$   (the log-odds)"); ax.set_ylabel("$p$")
ax.set_ylim(-.06, 1.12)
plt.show()
```

::: {.warn}
The slope is **not constant**. That is why one coefficient does not translate into one change in
probability.
:::

## Three ways to report one coefficient

| Quantity | Formula | Use when |
|---|---|---|
| Log-odds | $\beta_j$ | reporting the raw model |
| **Odds ratio** | $e^{\beta_j}$ | a credit or clinical audience |
| **Average marginal effect** | $\frac1n\sum_i \beta_j\, p_i(1-p_i)$ | **reporting to economists** |

::: {.check}
The odds ratio is constant everywhere; the probability change is not. Report the average marginal
effect unless you have a reason not to.
:::

# 5 · Reading the output {background-color="#16181A" style="color:#F7F6F3"}

## Fit it

```python
import numpy as np
import statsmodels.formula.api as smf

m = smf.logit("default ~ fico + int_rate + np.log(revol_bal + 1)",
              data=loans).fit()
print(m.summary().tables[1])
```

Line by line:

::: {.tight}
- `smf.logit` — the formula interface; `default ~ ...` reads "default explained by"
- `np.log(revol_bal + 1)` — transformed **inside** the formula, so the transformation is part of the
  recorded model rather than a step you might forget
- `+ 1` because balances of exactly zero exist, and $\log 0$ is undefined
:::

## What it says

```{python}
tbl = pd.DataFrame({"coef": m.params, "std err": m.bse,
                    "z": m.tvalues, "P>|z|": m.pvalues}).round(4)
tbl.index = ["Intercept", "fico", "int_rate", "log(revol_bal+1)"]
print(tbl.to_string())
```

::: {.check}
`fico` is **negative** — a better score lowers default risk. `int_rate` is strongly **positive**:
the platform's own pricing already encodes who is risky.
:::

## Make it reportable

```python
np.exp(m.params["fico"])     # 0.9936  — odds ratio per FICO point
m.get_margeff().summary()    # average marginal effects
```

::: {.check}
**0.9936** per point sounds like nothing. Per **100** points it is $0.9936^{100} \approx 0.52$ —
the odds of default roughly **halve**.
:::

::: {.warn}
The model does not care about units; your sentence does. Always say *per what*.
:::

# 6 · Why accuracy lies {background-color="#16181A" style="color:#F7F6F3"}

## The null model is already good

16% default. So the model *"nobody ever defaults"* — which uses no data at all — is

> **84% accurate.**

::: {.warn}
Report 85% accuracy and you have bought **one point** over saying nothing. Under imbalance, accuracy
measures the base rate, not skill.
:::

## Two curves, one model

```{python}
fpr, tpr, _ = roc_curve(y, p)
pre, rec, _ = precision_recall_curve(y, p)

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(7.8, 3.0))
a = axes[0]
a.plot(fpr, tpr, color=CL.accent, lw=2.2)
a.plot([0, 1], [0, 1], ls="--", color=CL.muted, lw=1)
a.text(.56, .30, "chance", color=CL.muted, fontsize=8.5, rotation=30)
a.set_title(f"ROC — AUC {roc_auc_score(y, p):.3f}")
a.set_xlabel("false positive rate"); a.set_ylabel("true positive rate")

b = axes[1]
b.plot(rec, pre, color=CL.accent, lw=2.2)
b.axhline(BASE, ls="--", color=CL.warn, lw=1.4)
b.text(.30, BASE + .02, f"baseline = base rate  {BASE:.3f}", color=CL.warn, fontsize=8.5)
b.set_ylim(0, .6)
b.set_title(f"Precision–Recall — AP {average_precision_score(y, p):.3f}")
b.set_xlabel("recall"); b.set_ylabel("precision")
plt.show()
```

## Read them against each other

::: {.tight}
- **ROC AUC 0.627** — looks like a working model. Its reference line is *chance*, a low bar.
- **PR AUC 0.232** — its reference line is the **base rate, 0.160**. The real gain is 0.232 against
  0.160.
:::

::: {.check}
Under heavy imbalance, **report PR with its baseline.** ROC flatters, because the false-positive
denominator is enormous.
:::

# 7 · The threshold {background-color="#16181A" style="color:#F7F6F3"}

## 0.5 is a claim, not a default

Classifying at $\hat p > 0.5$ asserts that a **false positive and a false negative cost the same**.

For a lender they do not: refusing a good borrower costs a **margin**; funding a defaulter costs the
**principal**.

## The cost-optimal threshold

$$\boxed{\;\tau^\star = \frac{c_{FP}}{c_{FP} + c_{FN}}\;}$$

```{python}
ratios = np.array([1, 2, 5, 10, 20])
taus = 1 / (1 + ratios)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7.2, 2.7))
ax.plot(ratios, taus, "o-", color=CL.accent, lw=2.2)
ax.axhline(.5, ls=":", color=CL.warn, lw=1.3)
ax.text(11.5, .53, "the software default, 0.5", color=CL.warn, fontsize=8.5)
for r, t in zip(ratios, taus):
    ax.annotate(f"{t:.2f}", (r, t), textcoords="offset points",
                xytext=(0, 9), ha="center", fontsize=9, color=CL.ink, fontweight="600")
ax.set_xlabel("cost of a miss relative to a false alarm   $c_{FN}:c_{FP}$")
ax.set_ylabel(r"$\tau^\star$"); ax.set_ylim(0, .64)
plt.show()
```

::: {.warn}
At a 5:1 cost ratio the right threshold is **0.167**, not 0.5.
:::

## What the threshold does to the decision

```{python}
ths = np.linspace(0.02, 0.6, 140)
flagged = np.array([(p >= t).mean() for t in ths])
recall  = np.array([((p >= t) & (y == 1)).sum() / y.sum() for t in ths])

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.plot(ths, flagged, color=CL.warn, lw=2.3)
ax.plot(ths, recall, color=CL.good, lw=2.3)
ax.axvline(1/6, color=CL.accent, ls="--", lw=1.5)
ax.text(1/6 + .01, .95, r"$\tau^\star = 0.167$  at 5:1", color=CL.accent, fontsize=8.5)
ax.text(.33, .20, "share of applications flagged", color=CL.warn, fontsize=8.5, fontweight="600")
ax.text(.33, .52, "share of defaults caught", color=CL.good, fontsize=8.5, fontweight="600")
ax.axvline(.5, color=CL.muted, ls=":", lw=1.2)
ax.text(.505, .06, "0.5 → nothing flagged", color=CL.muted, fontsize=8.5)
ax.set_xlabel("threshold"); ax.set_ylabel("share"); ax.set_ylim(0, 1.03)
plt.show()
```

## The number that should alarm you

```{python}
rows = []
for t in [0.10, 0.167, 0.20, 0.30, 0.50]:
    yh = (p >= t).astype(int)
    rows.append((t, int(yh.sum()), ((yh == 1) & (y == 1)).sum() / y.sum()))
out = pd.DataFrame(rows, columns=["threshold", "flagged", "recall"])
print(out.to_string(index=False, float_format=lambda v: f"{v:.3f}"))
```

::: {.warn}
**At 0.50 the model flags nothing at all.** Every applicant approved, recall zero — and the software
reported no error whatsoever.
:::

## Is 0.3 really 30%?

```{python}
frac, mean_pred = calibration_curve(y, p, n_bins=8, strategy="quantile")
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5.4, 3.1))
ax.plot([0, .5], [0, .5], ls="--", color=CL.muted, lw=1.2)
ax.plot(mean_pred, frac, "o-", color=CL.accent, lw=2.2)
ax.text(.28, .24, "perfectly calibrated", color=CL.muted, fontsize=8.5, rotation=36)
ax.set_xlabel("mean predicted probability"); ax.set_ylabel("observed frequency")
ax.set_xlim(0, .5); ax.set_ylim(0, .5)
plt.show()
```

::: {.check}
**Discrimination and calibration are different properties.** A model can rank perfectly and still be
miscalibrated — and a miscalibrated probability cannot enter a cost calculation.
:::

# 8 · A second example {background-color="#16181A" style="color:#F7F6F3"}

## Portugal's red wines

1,599 red *vinho verde* wines, chemically assayed, each rated by at least three blind tasters.

```python
wine = pd.read_parquet("data/redwines.parquet")
m_w  = smf.logit("good ~ alcohol + volatile_acidity + sulphates",
                 data=wine).fit()
np.exp(m_w.params["alcohol"])     # 2.74
```

::: {.check}
An odds ratio of **2.74**: each extra percentage point of alcohol nearly **triples** the odds a
taster calls the wine good.
:::

## Same method, very different signal

```{python}
m_w = smf.logit("good ~ alcohol + volatile_acidity + sulphates", data=wine).fit(disp=0)
pw = m_w.predict(wine).to_numpy(); yw = wine["good"].to_numpy()
f1, t1, _ = roc_curve(y, p); f2, t2, _ = roc_curve(yw, pw)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5.6, 3.2))
ax.plot([0, 1], [0, 1], ls="--", color=CL.muted, lw=1)
ax.plot(f1, t1, color=CL.warn, lw=2.4)
ax.plot(f2, t2, color=CL.good, lw=2.4)
ax.text(.50, .36, f"Lending Club   {roc_auc_score(y, p):.3f}",
        color=CL.warn, fontsize=9, fontweight="600")
ax.text(.26, .82, f"Red wines   {roc_auc_score(yw, pw):.3f}",
        color=CL.good, fontsize=9, fontweight="600")
ax.set_xlabel("false positive rate"); ax.set_ylabel("true positive rate")
plt.show()
```

## Why the difference is not the method

| | Lending Club | Red wines |
|---|---|---|
| $n$ | 9,578 | 1,599 |
| Base rate | 0.160 | 0.136 |
| ROC AUC | 0.627 | **0.866** |

::: {.check}
Same estimator, both imbalanced. **The predictors differ in how much they know.** Chemistry measures
the thing being judged; a credit file measures a person's past, not their next three years.
:::

::: {.warn}
When a model performs badly, ask what the features could possibly contain **before** reaching for a
fancier algorithm.
:::

# 9 · Key takeaways {background-color="#16181A" style="color:#F7F6F3"}

## What to carry out of this session

::: {.tight}
1. **A model gives a probability; a decision needs a threshold.** Separate acts, separate evidence.
2. **Report the base rate first.** Accuracy cannot be read without it.
3. **Report an odds ratio or an average marginal effect**, with its units.
4. **Derive the threshold from a stated cost ratio** — and show how the answer moves if it is wrong.
5. **Check calibration** before any probability enters a cost calculation.
6. **A weak model may be a weak feature set.** Look there before changing algorithm.
:::

## What loses marks reliably

| | |
|---|---|
| Accuracy on an imbalanced problem | It measures the base rate |
| Threshold silently left at 0.5 | An economic assumption, unstated |
| ROC AUC alone under imbalance | Hides the false positives |
| Random K-fold on a panel | Optimistic, for Session 04's reason |
| "The model found the drivers of default" | It found predictors |

## In the practice session

::: {.tight}
1. Fit penalised logistic on **your project**, grouped CV, base rate reported first
2. Produce a reliability diagram — is $\hat p$ usable as a probability?
3. State a cost ratio, derive $\tau^\star$, report precision and recall **there**
4. Bootstrap the selection; report frequencies, not one list
:::
